feed.title: Web & Frontend — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: An annotated directory of links on software, AI, security and science. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Docusaurus
entry.summary: Meta’s React-based documentation-site generator, with versioning and translation built in. Unlike general static generators it is docs-first: it ships ready-made pieces like version archives and i18n aimed specifically at software documentation.

entry.title: Hugo
entry.summary: A static-site generator written in Go that turns Markdown into websites. Unlike Node-based generators its distinction is raw speed: it builds thousands of pages in seconds, from a single binary, with no JS dependency tree.

entry.title: Obsidian Digital Garden
entry.summary: An Obsidian plugin that publishes notes straight into a live digital garden. Unlike generators such as Quartz it needs no build step: you publish from inside a note with one button, with no separate build pipeline to set up.

entry.title: Quartz
entry.summary: A generator that turns Markdown notes — Obsidian vaults especially — into a linked site. Unlike general static generators it preserves bidirectional links and backlinks: it publishes your digital garden with its network structure intact.

entry.title: 30 Seconds of Code
entry.summary: Code snippets short enough to read and understand in thirty seconds, for JavaScript, Python, React and CSS. Against Stack Overflow, each one is explained, tested and filed by topic — you browse it rather than search it.

entry.title: Can I Use
entry.summary: A table of which browser version supports which web feature, weighted by usage share. Where MDN explains the feature, this answers "can I ship it" at version and market-share level — it is where you decide whether a polyfill is needed.

entry.title: Checklist Design
entry.summary: Per-component checklists for buttons, forms, tables and the rest: which states to draw, which accessibility detail everyone forgets. Unlike a design-system doc it imposes no component library — it hands you a list to audit your own against.

entry.title: CodeToGo
entry.summary: Up-to-date one-line answers to everyday JavaScript questions like "how do I reverse an array". The difference from Stack Overflow is that the answer is not from 2012 — these are kept current with modern syntax.

entry.title: CSS-Tricks Snippets
entry.summary: An archive of snippets for CSS, HTML, JavaScript and .htaccess built up over years. Against scattered blog posts each snippet has its own page and discussion — and the comments usually hold a better version.

entry.title: Easing Wizard
entry.summary: A visual builder for CSS easing curves that covers not just cubic-bezier but linear() spring and bounce curves. That linear() support is what dates it past cubic-bezier.com: spring animation in CSS no longer needs a library.

entry.title: Howler.js
entry.summary: A cross-browser audio library that uses the Web Audio API and falls back to HTML5 Audio. Against hand-rolling Web Audio, it handles audio sprites, pooling and the mobile autoplay lock for you — the three things that always bite.

entry.title: Ladybird
entry.summary: An independent browser engine written from scratch, derived from neither Chromium, WebKit nor Gecko. That is precisely what separates it from the other "alternative" browsers, which are Chromium shells. Not yet ready for daily use.

entry.title: Land-book
entry.summary: A curated gallery of well-designed websites, filterable by industry, style and colour. Unlike award sites such as Awwwards it collects real shipping product sites rather than showpiece experiments.

entry.title: Lucide
entry.summary: An icon library of over 1,600 SVG icons with ready packages for React, Vue and Svelte. It is the community fork of Feather, and the difference is that it kept growing while Feather went quiet — and that it tree-shakes down to the icons you import.

entry.title: Splide
entry.summary: A dependency-free, accessibility-first slider and carousel library. It is markedly smaller than Swiper (~12KB gzipped) and gets keyboard navigation and ARIA roles right by default — the usual weak spot of carousels.

entry.title: TeleportHQ
entry.summary: A low-code platform that turns a visual interface design into clean React, Vue or HTML. Against Webflow the output is exportable, readable component code — you can take the design over and keep building by hand.

entry.title: Uiverse
entry.summary: A community-contributed gallery of open-source UI elements: buttons, cards, loaders, toggles. Unlike CodePen, everything is MIT-licensed, copy-paste ready and offered as plain CSS or Tailwind, with no framework attached.

entry.title: Wakamai Fondue
entry.summary: Drop in a font file and it reports everything inside: character set, OpenType features, variable axes — plus the CSS that switches each of them on. Unlike a font previewer, the output is code you can paste.

entry.title: WebAIM
entry.summary: The accessibility centre at Utah State University — the contrast checker, the WAVE tool and the annual "Million" survey all come from here. Where the WCAG spec states the rule, WebAIM shows what applying it actually looks like.

entry.title: CSS-Tricks
entry.summary: Two decades of CSS technique, whose Flexbox and Grid guides became the de facto references. Faster than the spec when you are hunting a specific layout problem.

entry.title: Flexbox Froggy
entry.summary: The Flexbox sibling of Grid Garden, teaching alignment by positioning frogs. It settles the justify-content versus align-items confusion in twenty minutes.

entry.title: Grid Garden
entry.summary: A 28-level game teaching CSS Grid by watering carrots. Properties like grid-column and grid-area stick when you type them rather than read them.

entry.title: W3C Markup Validation
entry.summary: Checks HTML against the spec, surfacing unclosed tags and invalid nesting that browsers quietly repair. A share of accessibility problems begins right there.

entry.title: HTML Reference
entry.summary: Every HTML element and attribute with a visual example, scannable on one page. It lacks MDN’s depth but answers “what did this tag do again” faster.

entry.title: Web Dev for Beginners
entry.summary: A 24-lesson curriculum with a quiz before and after each lesson and a project at the end. That structure is what lets you measure progress when studying alone.

entry.title: Foundation for Sites
entry.summary: The long-running alternative to Bootstrap: a responsive front-end framework with an XY grid, accessibility-minded components and a separate edition for HTML email. Against Bootstrap it imposes fewer visual opinions — components arrive unstyled and you bring the design. Caveat: the last release was September 2024 and the last push January 2025. The project is not archived, but it has been dormant for two years and its marketing site still advertises a webinar from 2017.

entry.title: Snap.svg
entry.summary: A JavaScript library for generating and animating SVG, written as Raphaël’s successor for modern browsers. Against D3 it is not about data visualisation but about composing SVG directly — you produce graphics, not charts.

entry.title: Maps Tracker
entry.summary: Measures Google Maps ranking across a grid of locations, showing how the same query shifts block by block — precisely the blind spot of general SEO tools.

entry.title: SEO Kriterleri
entry.summary: A technical SEO checklist covering heading structure, schema markup and page speed in actionable terms — one of the Turkish resources furthest from marketing talk.

entry.title: before.click
entry.summary: An archive of App Store screenshot designs. Store-page conversion hangs directly on these images, which makes it a narrow but well-aimed resource.

entry.title: Site of Sites
entry.summary: A gallery for whole-site design language, collecting sites with strong typography and motion.

entry.title: Unsection
entry.summary: Design examples organised by section — hero, pricing, FAQ, footer — filterable so you solve one section instead of scanning whole sites.

entry.title: GrapesJS
entry.summary: A visual page editor you embed in your own product, defining the component and style managers yourself. Unlike hosted site builders, you own the editor.

entry.title: Bootstrap
entry.summary: Ready components and a grid system that get you a working interface without design decisions. The cost is that a Bootstrap site is recognisable from a distance.

entry.title: Shopify Liquid
entry.summary: The object, filter and tag reference for Shopify’s theme language — where you find which data is reachable from which template when building a store theme.

entry.title: htmx
entry.summary: Attributes fire requests and swap the returned HTML fragment into the page — no JSON, no client state. 14 kB with no dependencies, and a sane exit where SPA complexity is not warranted.

entry.title: Tailwind CSS
entry.summary: You style with utility classes and the build step drops unused ones, so the CSS file stops growing. Bootstrap hands you components; this hands you building blocks.

entry.title: Angular
entry.summary: Routing, forms, HTTP and dependency injection ship inside the framework. In React you pick each one; here the decisions are made for you, and flexibility narrows accordingly.

entry.title: React
entry.summary: The rewritten official docs, centred on hooks with class components gone. The “You Might Not Need an Effect” page targets the single most common mistake head on.

entry.title: The Modern JavaScript Tutorial
entry.summary: Works the language front to back without skipping the hard parts: prototype chain, event loop, promises. MDN is the reference and this is the tutorial; they complement each other.
